title: The December Payment Freeze: Why Your Best Corporate Clients Go Quiet for Six Weeks
excerpt: Many large clients quietly pause payment runs for six to eight weeks every December. Here is how to see the gap coming and forecast around it before it hits your bank balance in January.
content:
Most Australian businesses close out November with a strong number. Invoices are out, the work is delivered, and the sales pipeline is pushing hard into the last productive weeks before Christmas. What gets far less attention is what happens to collections once the biggest clients on that debtor list close their accounts payable function for the year.

Large corporate customers, government departments and many franchise head offices run their final payment cycle of the calendar year in the first half of December, then do not process another payment run until late January. For the business sitting on the supplier side of that relationship, work delivered and invoiced in November can sit unpaid for six to eight weeks, not because the client disputes a dollar of it, but because there is simply nobody left at their end to approve it before the new year.

This happens every December, and most owner-led businesses still treat it as a run of bad luck rather than a pattern that can be read and planned around in advance. The better time to look at this is now, while there is still a working week or two left to act on it, not in the third week of January when the bank balance quietly fails to match a strong sales result.

The freeze is structural, not personal

The pattern we typically see across businesses that rely on a handful of larger customers is straightforward. Accounts payable teams go on leave in mid December. Approval chains that rely on one or two signatures break down the moment either signatory is out of office. Finance systems that batch payment runs weekly or fortnightly simply stop batching until the office reopens. None of this reflects how the client feels about the relationship or the quality of the work delivered. It is a seasonal mechanical gap, the same one every supplier in that client's ecosystem is sitting inside at the same time.

Recognising the freeze as structural rather than personal matters, because it changes what a business does in response. Chasing harder in the third week of December rarely moves the date forward. Knowing the date in advance changes what else gets planned around it.

What the freeze actually costs

Wages, rent, loan repayments and the superannuation guarantee due on 28 January do not pause for anyone else's payment run. A business that is owed a genuinely strong month of revenue can still find itself drawing on an overdraft, delaying a supplier payment, or asking a director for a short term top up, purely because the timing of cash in and cash out has come apart. None of that shows up as a profit problem. The cash flow discipline most businesses practise during the rest of the year, forecasting a few weeks ahead and reacting to what the bank balance shows, simply was not built for a six to eight week gap that arrives at the same time every year.

The businesses that feel this hardest tend to be the ones where one or two large clients make up a disproportionate share of the debtor book. A single government contract, head office account or anchor customer going quiet for six weeks has a very different effect on a business with three major clients than it does on one with thirty smaller accounts.

Reading the calendar before the freeze starts

The practical fix starts with a question most businesses never ask directly: what date does each major client's accounts payable team process its final run of the year, and when does the first run of the new year land. That single date, not the invoice due date written into the contract, is the number that actually determines when the cash arrives. Once it is known, invoicing can be brought forward to clear that cut off rather than drift past it by a few days and fall into the six week gap by accident.

This is exactly the kind of forward visibility a rolling 13-week cash flow forecast is built to surface. Mapping known receivable timing against known outgoings, wages, rent, loan repayments, the January superannuation guarantee due date, turns a vague sense that December is always tight into a specific, fundable number with weeks of notice attached to it, rather than a surprise that shows up in the bank balance in the new year.

A concentration problem wearing a seasonal disguise

For a Brisbane professional services or trade business built around three or four large customers, the December freeze is also a quieter version of a bigger question worth asking at some point: what happens to this business if any one of those relationships changes meaningfully, not just slows down for six weeks. A Brisbane based business carrying that concentration risk usually already senses it, even before the Christmas payment gap makes it visible in the bank account.

None of this requires a different client relationship or an awkward conversation in December. It requires knowing the dates in advance and building the forecast around them before the freeze starts, not after. If those dates are not mapped yet, there is still time to fix that before the office closes for the year, and a discovery call is a reasonable place to start.

faqs.q: Why do big companies stop paying invoices in December in Australia?
faqs.a: It is rarely a dispute over the invoice itself. Accounts payable teams reduce staff over the Christmas period, approval chains built around one or two signatures stop functioning once those people are on leave, and payment runs that batch weekly simply pause until the office reopens in late January. The pattern is seasonal and structural, not a comment on the relationship or the work delivered.

faqs.q: How much cash buffer should a small business hold before the Christmas payment freeze?
faqs.a: There is no single figure that fits every business, because it depends on how much of the debtor book sits with clients who pause payments over December. The more useful exercise is mapping exactly which invoices are exposed to the freeze and for how many weeks, then holding enough buffer to cover wages, rent and loan repayments across that specific gap rather than guessing at a round number.

faqs.q: Can invoicing earlier in November help avoid the December payment freeze?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Once a client's final payment run date for the year is known, invoicing can be brought forward to clear that cut off with a buffer of a few days, rather than drifting past it and falling into the six to eight week gap by accident. Building this into a cash flow discipline that runs year round makes the timing easier to catch early.

faqs.q: What does a 13-week cash flow forecast show that a bank balance does not?
faqs.a: A bank balance shows where cash sits today. A rolling 13-week cash flow forecast maps known receivable timing against known outgoings including wages, rent, loan repayments and the January superannuation guarantee due date, so a seasonal gap like the December payment freeze shows up as a specific, fundable number weeks in advance rather than a surprise in January.

faqs.q: Does the December payment freeze affect businesses in Sydney and Melbourne too?
faqs.a: Yes. The pattern is tied to how large corporate customers, government departments and franchise head offices run their payment cycles, not to any one state. A Sydney business supplying a handful of large accounts, or a Melbourne business in the same position, faces the same structural gap as one in Brisbane or regional Queensland.

faqs.q: Should a business chase overdue invoices harder in December or wait until January?
faqs.a: Chasing harder in the third week of December rarely moves the payment date forward if the client's accounts payable function has already closed for the year. The more productive move is confirming the exact resumption date in January and timing follow up for the days just before it, while using the quieter weeks to get the rest of the financial forecasting and cash position in order.
